findings: fetchLivePrice recurses on ANY caught error with no maximum attempt count, no backoff/jitter, and no distinction between transient and permanent failures (e.g. HTTP 429/5xx vs a 400/404 for an invalid or missing sku). For any permanently-failing order (a null/undefined order.sku, a delisted SKU, a malformed request) this becomes an infinite retry loop that never resolves or rejects, which directly explains 'occasionally times out entirely' rather than the request ever cleanly failing.

pricingApi has no timeout configured (acknowledged in the code's own comment). A hung/slow upstream call never throws, so the try/catch retry logic never even engages — the await simply blocks forever. This means the retry mechanism gives a false sense of resilience: the actual unbounded-latency failure mode (a stalled TCP connection or a pricingApi instance that accepts but never responds) is not retried, it is just hung on indefinitely.

getDashboard fetches prices serially inside a for-await loop instead of concurrently (e.g. Promise.all(orders.map(...))), even though each fetchLivePrice call is independent (keyed only by order.sku with no cross-iteration data dependency). This multiplies latency linearly by order count and, combined with the unbounded retry issue, means a single stuck order blocks every subsequent order in the same request from ever being processed — the whole response hangs, not just that one item.

Under load this becomes a genuine cascading-failure/retry-storm mechanism, matching the 'performance cascade' framing: if pricingApi is already slow or rate-limiting due to load, every erroring call immediately retries with no backoff, so each dashboard request (across N orders) and every concurrent user's dashboard request all hammer pricingApi harder in direct response to it already struggling — amplifying the very condition causing the errors and pushing it further into degradation/outage rather than shedding load.

The orders query (`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=$1`) has no LIMIT/pagination, so a user with a large order history linearly multiplies both the serial-latency problem and the exposure to the infinite-retry hang — there is no cap on how many external pricingApi round trips (each potentially unbounded) a single dashboard request can trigger.

There is no per-order isolation or fallback: a single order whose SKU price lookup fails permanently (e.g., a discontinued product no longer in pricingApi) prevents the entire dashboard from ever returning, instead of degrading gracefully (e.g., returning the order with a null/stale price and continuing). This turns a partial, expected data issue into a full endpoint outage.
